commits.summary: Ship the JDK models inside jvmcontract: the boxing caches, a generated Character.digit and java.nio.charset, on JBMC's class path and in the interpreter, replacing the models-library fork (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract's proofs relied on two things outside the tool: JBMC's view of the class library, which is empty beyond six real JDK classes, and a hand-cloned fork of the CProver models library in libs/ whose four charset classes, together with lib/jbmc-models, had to be compiled by hand and passed on --classpath before a proof over a class like Commons Codec's Hex gave anything but an artifact (example 109). The models are now a first-class part of the tool. lib/models/ holds their Java sources (the four boxing caches, the four java.nio.charset classes from the fork under their OpenJDK header, and a new java.lang.Character with digit, isDigit and forDigit generated by lib/models/tools/GenerateCharacter.java from the running JDK's decimal-digit table as 80 comparisons, no loops, no tables), lib/models/build.sh compiles them with javac --release 8 into lib/models/classes/, which are committed and embedded in the binary by lib/src/models.rs; a unit test compiles the sources afresh and compares the disassembly, so a stale class file fails the build. equivalence and prove write the models into their working directory and put them last on JBMC's class path (--no-models leaves them out); jvmcontract models lists them and --write DIR writes them out. The interpreter executes a model's bytecode for the methods the model defines, ahead of its natives (ClassPath::bytecode, bytecode_method and Origin::Model; a model is never an application class and its shape is consulted only where neither the application nor the JDK image has the class, so capability, API and behavioural contracts are unchanged), which also fixes its Character.digit and isDigit, which used Rust's ASCII-only and is_numeric tables.

Two JBMC settings changed with it. JBMC's string solver, on by default, replaces every call of java.lang.Character by an approximation of its own ahead of any class on the class path, and gave digit an arbitrary result (the 'wrong answer' on digit(U+0660, 16) recorded in example 109 was the solver's, not the tables'), so JBMC now runs with --no-refine-strings (--refine-strings turns it back on). With the string solver off JBMC's MiniSAT path stalled for over ten minutes on the binary-search proof over eight elements that took a second before, while its bundled CaDiCaL settles every stage in about a second, so JBMC is asked for cadical by default (--sat-solver; a build that answers 'unknown solver' is run again with its default). lib/jbmc-models and libs/README.md are gone; the clone of the fork stays ignored; the verification pipeline no longer links it into exports; lib/README.md, lib/models/README.md (the catalogue, where each model is used, how to add one, the licence), examples/README.md, example 109's record and the verify-bytecode skill's reference say what changed.

Verified inline: cargo test passes (58 unit tests, 27 integration tests, in 46 s where the suite had been timing out on the MiniSAT path), among them two new tests: the interpreter runs Character.digit, the StandardCharsets static initializer, Charset.forName and its exception from the models, and JBMC proves Character.digit's range over every char on the model, refutes a stricter claim with a Unicode digit the interpreter replays on the same model, proves Integer.valueOf round-trips through the cache model, and fails to verify the same without --no-models. The release binary builds; jvmcontract models lists ten classes. Verification pending: job 20261103-010716-jdk-models-shipped-with-jvmcontract-the (the library's JBMC tests under the pipeline) and job 20261103-010716-example-109-revisited-hex-todigit-s-regr (the regression proof of Hex#toDigit between the two commons-codec commits with the Character model, which example 109 could not make), both in verification/jobs/.

commits.summary: Add the tool's own bounded model checker: the harness executed symbolically over bit-vectors and decided by a bundled CaDiCaL, behind --engine native and auto (verification pending)
commits.body:
JBMC is the second external dependency the proofs rest on, and its limits are the ones that have bitten: no models of the class library, a string solver that overrides the class path, a MiniSAT path that stalls, no option that shortens a run. lib/src/bmc is the start of the replacement, inside jvmcontract. bits.rs bit-blasts the JVM's int and long arithmetic into circuits over propositional literals fed to the cadical crate (CaDiCaL compiled by cc; the dev profile builds it optimised, since the tests run the solver): addition, two's-complement multiplication, Java's truncating division and remainder (MIN_VALUE / -1 wraps), shifts masked as the JVM masks them, signed and unsigned comparison, conversions, with constant folding and gate hashing so that the same function of the same inputs is one variable and two copies of a circuit, the method's and the harness's, fold together. mod.rs executes the generated harness class, the same one JBMC is given, one path at a time: fresh bits for each parameter in its range, feasibility of both sides of every branch asked of the solver, loops unwound up to --unwind, exceptions thrown and caught by class through the handler tables (division by zero and the Math.*Exact overflows as exception paths), calls into the application and into the tool's JDK models inlined, Math's exact and floor operations and the wrappers' comparisons as circuits, strings and other objects as opaque values. A path that reaches the harness's AssertionError on a satisfiable condition is a violation whose input the model names; every path returning or infeasible is a proof. Arrays, floating point, static state beyond compile-time constants and other JDK calls are refused with a reason.

prove and equivalence take --engine jbmc (the default, unchanged), native (the tool's own checker, a refusal being unverifiable) or auto (the tool's own where the harness is in its fragment, JBMC elsewhere with a note: line saying why). The engine's result takes the shape of a JBMC result, so a violation is replayed and shrunk in the interpreter exactly as JBMC's is, which also means an engine mistake on a violation shows as 'does not reproduce' rather than as a false witness. lib/README.md has a section on the checker, its fragment and what it does not do yet (arrays, path merging, floating point); the skill reference and the models catalogue mention the flag.

Verified inline: cargo test passes (66 unit tests, 28 integration tests). The circuit tests compare every operation with Rust's integer semantics on the edge cases of int and long; the engine tests prove a tautology without a solver call, refute a * a >= 0 with an overflowing input, prove the division-by-zero path and a concrete quotient, hit the unwinding bound, and prove multiplyExact's overflow condition and refute a claim that addExact never throws; the integration test the_tools_own_checker_agrees_with_jbmc_on_integer_proofs runs eight property proofs and three regression proofs on the fixtures with both checkers and requires the same verdicts (and the same shrunk witness where it is unique), and checks that auto hands an array proof to JBMC with the note. Verification pending: job 20261103-015449-the-tool-s-own-bounded-model-checker-uni (the suite under the pipeline) and job 20261103-015449-the-tool-s-own-checker-on-the-quorum-and (the Quorum and Crosscut property contracts under --engine auto against --engine jbmc, property by property), both in verification/jobs/.

commits.summary: Let the feature loop be stopped after the current cycle by typing stop in its terminal
commits.body: feature-loop.sh now reads its terminal in the background while claude works (claude gets /dev/null as input so they don't compete). Typing stop (or q) and Enter makes the loop exit 0 after the cycle under way has committed and compacted; resume withdraws the request, and touching $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/feature-loop.stop does the same from another terminal or when there is no terminal. A stale stop file is cleared at start and on exit. Documented in llm-dlc/README.md. Verified with stubbed claude and jj under a pseudo-terminal: stop mid-cycle ended after that cycle, resume let it continue, and the stop file worked with stdin from /dev/null.

commits.summary: Give the feature loop a cycle count, adjustable while it runs, in place of the stop command
commits.body: feature-loop.sh takes an optional number of cycles after the prompt name (tla 5); without it the loop runs until stopped. While it runs it reads commands typed in its terminal: +N and -N add or remove cycles after the current one, =N or N sets how many remain, 0 or stop ends after the current cycle, inf removes the limit, and ? or help shows where it stands or the command list. The list is printed at start and a one-line reminder with the count at each cycle. The cycle under way always finishes, commit and compact included, and the loop exits 0 when the count reaches 0. The loop and the terminal reader share the count through a locked state file in XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, removed on exit; this replaces the stop/resume commands and stop file of the previous change. llm-dlc/README.md documents the commands in a table. Verified with stubbed claude and jj under a pseudo-terminal (the systemd scope step skipped): 2 cycles adjusted with +3 and -1 ran 4; unlimited with stop ran 2; -2 against no limit and unknown input were refused with help; 0 ended after cycle 1; no terminal with a count of 2 ran 2; bad arguments print usage and exit 2.

commits.summary: Add verification-loop.sh: a fresh Sonnet session runs /run-verification whenever the queue has work, and the loop watches for new jobs in between
commits.body: llm-dlc/tools/verification-loop.sh polls python3 verification/pipeline.py status (every 60 s, VERIFICATION_LOOP_POLL). When jobs are pending that this machine can run, or results wait to be collected, it starts a new claude -p session on claude-sonnet-5-5 with the run-verification skill and an instruction to work until the queue is clear without asking anything; each run has a fresh context. A run that leaves work behind (such as resubmitted jobs) is followed by another, up to 4 in a row (VERIFICATION_LOOP_RUNS); a run that leaves exactly what it found is not repeated until the queue changes. Jobs too big for the runner and jobs another runner holds don't start a run. Typed commands: stop, now, ?, listed at start and reminded at each run. log and the stream-json display moved to llm-dlc/tools/loop-common.sh, shared with feature-loop.sh, and the display now shows background task completions. Documented in llm-dlc/README.md (section renamed Unattended loops) and verification/README.md. Verified first that a headless claude -p session waits for a background command's notification before exiting (the skill runs the pipeline in the background). Then with a fake pipeline.py and claude: a cleared queue goes idle and a new job starts a second run; a run with no progress waits; deferred-only jobs start nothing; runs that keep resubmitting stop at the cap; stop while idle exits 0. The queue parser was checked against the real status (8 runnable jobs), and feature-loop.sh rerun with stubs after the refactor.

commits.summary: Add boundary contracts (B12): a Spring Boot module's routes, listeners, schedules, bean definitions and configuration keys, the advice on each bean, and the places where an annotation does not do what it says, read from the class files (verification pending)
commits.body: What changed: the class-file reader now parses RuntimeVisibleAnnotations, RuntimeVisibleParameterAnnotations, the Exceptions attribute and generic Signature attributes (lib/src/classfile/annotations.rs, signature.rs). A new contract kind, boundaries.contract (lib/src/boundaries.rs), lists every bean with framework annotations (Spring, Jakarta Validation and Transactions, Resilience4j, Micrometer), one line per entry point with its route composed from the class and method mappings, the handler's signature with its parameter annotations and generic types, @ConfigurationProperties keys in Boot's relaxed form, and the advice on each member as indented lines. It then checks what the framework will do with each annotation and records the places where it does nothing as '!' lines: a @Transactional or @PreAuthorize method called on 'this' from the same bean (the receiver is found by a backwards walk over the bytecode's stack effects, lambdas included), advice on a private, static or final method or a final class, a @Transactional method whose declared checked exception commits because rollbackFor does not name it, an @Async method whose non-Future result is lost, a @Cacheable void method, a @Scheduled method with parameters, and constraints on a method that is neither a request handler nor on a @Validated bean. 'jvmcontract boundaries CLASSES' prints it, 'verify'/'update --add boundaries' check and write it like the capability and API contracts, with a boundaries-changed SARIF rule anchored to the first added member. Why: a Spring Boot service is mostly boundaries, none of which is in the code's control flow, so no unit test shows a dropped guard, a widened route, a changed rollback rule or a proxy that is bypassed; the contract makes them a one-line diff a reviewer approves, and the '!' lines are the Spring bugs experts know by name and still ship. Also: the three Box Office modules with Spring annotations carry their boundary contracts in src/contract, checked by a new boxoffice.boundaries Gradle convention (Exec, skipped when jvmcontract is not on the PATH); approach B12 in examples/approaches.md and the router; a B12 runner in build.py (Gradle compileJava of the patched copy, then jvmcontract verify); a spring-boot domain tag; example 110 (an Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders loses the body's @Valid, expected violation). How verified: new Spring fixtures under lib/tests/fixtures/spring (stand-in annotation types under the real package names) exercise every entry kind and every problem once, and the integration test checks the rendered contract line by line, the round trip through parse, the update/verify flow and that a dropped @PreAuthorize is reported as a violation anchored to the handler; 69 unit and 29 integration tests pass. Running the tool over the real ticketing-service, payment-service and messaging classes gives 19, 6 and 4 beans with 13, 3 and 9 entry points and no problems, as expected of a codebase with programmatic transactions. Verification pending: job 20261103-025524-example-110-an-idempotency-key-header-on runs example 110 through build.py, which needs Gradle.

commits.summary: Add wire types to boundary contracts: the JSON shape of each request, response and message as Jackson encodes it, with checks for a subtype missing from @JsonSubTypes, a type id that is a class name and a persistence type on the wire (verification pending)
commits.body:
A Spring Boot module's boundary contract now ends with its wire types (lib/src/wire.rs): one block per type reachable from the handlers' @RequestBody parameters and results, the message listeners' payloads and every Jackson-annotated class, followed through property types into the module and its sibling modules (the class path entries under --base) and stopped at library types. A block lists the properties as Jackson 3 finds them (record components; public fields, getters, setters and @JsonProperty members, superclasses included) under their wire names (@JsonProperty, @JsonNaming), with Bean Validation constraints before the type and a ? for a property that may be null or absent (Optional, @JsonInclude), enum constants with their @JsonProperty names or @JsonValue method, and for a polymorphic family the @JsonTypeInfo placement and each subtype's id. A renamed component, a dropped @JsonSubTypes entry or a new enum constant changes no signature and passes every test that uses the same classes on both sides; in the contract it is a changed line. The ! checks were established with a scratch program against the Jackson 3.1 jars Box Office uses: a permitted subtype of a sealed base that @JsonSubTypes does not list is written under its class name (Outer$Inner) and rejected when read back; a listed subtype without a name, or a permitted subtype of a base without @JsonSubTypes, gets the class name as its id; @JsonTypeInfo(use = CLASS) puts Java class names on the wire; an interface or abstract class without @JsonTypeInfo is written as the runtime class's properties with no id to read it back by; a bean with no visible properties is written as {}; two properties with one wire name; and a persistence type (@Document, @Entity, @Table) on the wire. The class-file reader gained a raw method_parts for signatures. A request type whose only framework annotations are its constraints is shown once, as a wire type.

Two bugs from the first boundary-contract commit are fixed on the way: update --add KIND with the contract file already present fell through to the method-target parser (the Gradle updateBoundaries tasks had never run), and the boxoffice.boundaries Gradle convention referenced the project at execution time, which Gradle's configuration cache refuses; it now captures plain values. update also leaves a module contract alone when nothing in it changed, so the Java tool's capabilities.contract in the contracts module keeps its header. The four Box Office contracts (ticketing-service, payment-service, messaging, and now contracts, whose wire types are the message families) were regenerated through ./gradlew updateBoundaries. The payment service's contract has a real ! line: GET /payments/{orderId} returns the Mongo PaymentDocument itself, gateway reference included; it is left as found and noted in the Box Office README.

Example 111 (B12, Box Office contracts module): a PaymentVoided record added to the sealed PaymentEvent family, published by the payment service and handled in ticketing where the compiler demands the new switch case, without its @JsonSubTypes entry. The change is intended, so the runner (build.py run_boundaries) regenerates the contract, records the diff, and reports a ! line the old contract did not have as the violation: a new rule for intended changes. Verified inline: 71 unit and 29 integration tests pass (the Spring fixtures gained Jackson stand-ins and types exercising every wire feature and problem once, asserted line by line, with a renamed component failing verify); the patched PaymentEvent compiled against the Jackson jars renders the expected ! line. Job 20261103-032834-example-111-a-paymentvoided-event-added runs the example through Gradle on the pipeline.

commits.summary: Add the configuration block to boundary contracts: the keys a module's classes read, the keys its application files set and the keys the class path's metadata declares, cross-checked, with ! lines for a key nothing binds, a deprecated key and a value of the wrong type (verification pending)
commits.body:
A Spring Boot module's boundary contract (B12) now has a configuration block between the beans and the wire types. lib/src/config.rs collects the keys from three places and compares them in Boot's relaxed canonical form: what the classes read (${key:default} placeholders in any annotation, the fields of a @ConfigurationProperties type under its prefix with nested types, lists as key[], maps as key.*, and a record's @DefaultValue; @ConditionalOnProperty; environment.getProperty with a constant key, found by the same stack walk that finds a self-invocation's receiver), what the application files under --resources set (application.yaml, profile files, --- profile documents, the config/ directory; a YAML subset reader of its own and a .properties reader), and what the configuration metadata on the class path declares (META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json, which every Spring Boot starter carries with types, sources and deprecations; ClassPath::resources reads a resource from every entry). Each key is one line with its type and the value per profile, or its default when no file sets it, and under it who reads it. The ! lines: a key set in a file that no class reads and no metadata declares, with the nearest known key named; a key the metadata marks deprecated, with its replacement and whether Boot still binds it; a value that is not of the key's type (integers, floating point, boolean, Duration, DataSize, Period, and an enum's constants resolved from the class path with relaxed matching); a placeholder default that is not. None of these fails a test, since tests do not run with the production profile and a missing key quietly takes its default. The stats line gains the count of configuration keys; the boundaries command takes --classpath and --resources, verify and update take --resources, and a finding on a configuration key is anchored to the line of the application file. The @ConfigurationProperties key lines of the bean block are gone, since the configuration block lists them with their values.

Verified with the library's Spring fixtures, which gain an application.yaml and application-prod.properties with each kind of problem once, a metadata file with a deprecated key and a map-typed one, and classes reading keys through @ConditionalOnProperty, Environment and a nested @ConfigurationProperties record: 76 unit tests and 29 integration tests pass, the boundary test asserting each configuration line, the verifier's up-to-date and changed paths and the anchoring to the YAML line. The four Box Office contracts were regenerated through Gradle, whose boundaries convention now passes the resource directories and whose java conventions gain a printRuntimeClasspath task; the ticketing service's block lists its 14 keys with the Spring Boot starters' declarations and the keys the imported messaging module reads, with no problems. A scratch application.yaml against the real ticketing classes and class path produced the expected five problems (a mistyped key with its nearest neighbour, a Duration written as words, a port written as a word, a key with no reader, spring.data.mongodb.uri deprecated in Boot 4). Example 112 appends a prod profile document to the ticketing service's application.yaml with boxoffice.hold.max-seat: 12, one letter from the key the code reads; the change is intended, so the regenerated contract's new ! line is the violation. Its Gradle run is queued as job 20261103-040613-example-112-a-prod-profile-sets-the-hold. A new defect tag, configuration-drift, covers it.

The verification session ran concurrently and its two preceding commits (the results of 8 jobs, and the Quorum resubmission) swept in earlier states of this change's files; this commit completes them, and in turn carries the results of job 20261103-025524-example-110, which that session wrote while this one worked.

commits.summary: Add validation checks to boundary contracts: the constraints inside a wire type's properties, and ! lines for a nested type no @Valid leads into, a body taken without @Valid, a group a @Valid or @Validated leaves out and a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract's boundary contract already listed the Bean Validation constraints on each property of a wire type. It now reads the constraints inside a type too (List<@NotBlank String>, from the class file's RuntimeVisibleTypeAnnotations, which the class file parser now reads, with a type tree in classfile/signature.rs to walk a type path) and checks them as Hibernate Validator will run them, in the new lib/src/validation.rs: a property whose type carries constraints that no @Valid on the property or inside its type leads into gets a ! line (Bean Validation does not cascade without one); a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (@Size on an int, which the compiler accepts and the first validation throws UnexpectedTypeException for) and a null check on a primitive get one; a @RequestBody taken without @Valid or @Validated while its type is constrained is a ! line on the handler, as is a @Valid, which validates the Default group, or a @Validated(G.class), which validates G and the groups it extends, on a body with constraints in other groups; and constraints on a private or static method of a @Validated bean are reported as not enforced, since method validation goes through the proxy. The built-in constraints are matched against the JDK type families they validate (Hibernate Validator's, which Spring Boot ships: Min and Max take a CharSequence too); a custom constraint, a type that cannot be found, @Pattern expressions and group sequences are not judged.

Verified with the library's Spring fixtures, which gain a Booking record with one of each case and a BookingsController taking it without @Valid, with @Valid and with @Validated(OnCreate.class), plus a private constrained method on the @Validated Quotas bean: 80 unit and 29 integration tests pass. The existing NotesController fixture turned out to take its Note body without @Valid, which the contract now reports. The four Box Office contracts were regenerated through Gradle: the ticketing service's CreateConcert and HoldSeats now show the type-use constraints on their lists that earlier contracts hid, and no module gains a problem. Example 113 adds a nested Billing record with @NotBlank fields to PlaceOrder as a @NotNull component without @Valid; its regenerated contract has the new ! line, confirmed by hand through Gradle, and its run is queued as job 20261103-044358-example-113-a-nested-billing-record-on-p. New defect tag validation-gap; docs in lib/README.md, approaches.md, the plugin reference and the Box Office README.

commits.summary: Add the activation block to boundary contracts: what switches each kind of annotation on (an @Enable annotation on a configuration in scope, an auto-configuration whose conditions hold, a Bean Validation provider), with a ! line for a family nothing enables (verification pending)
commits.body:
A Spring annotation is read only by the interceptor some switch registers: @Scheduled needs @EnableScheduling, @Async @EnableAsync, @Cacheable @EnableCaching, @PreAuthorize @EnableMethodSecurity (@Secured and @RolesAllowed its securedEnabled and jsr250Enabled), @Retryable @EnableRetry, an @Aspect @EnableAspectJAutoProxy; @Transactional, @KafkaListener, @RabbitListener, @JmsListener and method validation are switched on by Spring Boot's auto-configuration when its conditions hold, @Timed, @Counted and @Observed by aspect beans the AspectJ weaver makes possible, @Valid by a Bean Validation provider on the class path. Without the switch the code compiles, the context starts and every test that does not depend on the advice passes, while the method is never scheduled, cached or secured. The new lib/src/activation.rs adds an activation block to the boundary contract, between the beans and the configuration keys: the header names the application class and the packages it scans, and each family the module uses is a line naming what enables it and how that configuration is reached (local, imported by the application class, scanned from a dependency, auto-configured), or 'nothing enables it' with a ! line naming the nearest miss: a class that carries the switch but is not a component, a configuration outside the scanned packages, or an auto-configuration whose @ConditionalOnClass or @ConditionalOnResource fails. The configurations in scope follow Spring's rules as far as class files show them: local components in the scanned packages (meta-annotations followed), class-path classes in those packages, the @Import closure, nested static configuration classes, and the auto-configurations every jar's META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports and spring.factories list minus the application's excludes, with @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingClass, @ConditionalOnResource and @ConditionalOnWebApplication evaluated against the class path and the other conditions taken as met.

Verified by the library's unit tests (84) and integration tests (29): the Spring fixtures gained an application class (fixtures/spring/App.java), an imported configuration, one outside the scanned package, a non-component class carrying @EnableKafka, and four fake auto-configurations shaped like Boot's (a nested @EnableTransactionManagement class, a @ConditionalOnClass that fails, a @ConditionalOnResource provider check, an aspect bean behind the AspectJ weaver), listed in the fixtures' AutoConfiguration.imports with a ValidationProvider service file. The four Box Office contracts were regenerated through Gradle: the ticketing service shows @Scheduled enabled by MessagingConfiguration imported from the messaging module, @KafkaListener by KafkaAnnotationDrivenConfiguration.EnableKafkaConfiguration auto-configured, and @Valid by Hibernate Validator 9.1.3 on the class path; no module gains a problem. Example 114 puts @Cacheable on TicketingStore.concert with no @EnableCaching in scope; the regenerated contract's new ! line was confirmed by hand through Gradle, and the pipeline run is job 20261103-052906-example-114-a-cacheable-on-the-concert-l. New defect tag inert-annotation. Docs: lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the verify-bytecode reference and the Box Office README.

commits.summary: Add the stored types block to boundary contracts: the shape of each Spring Data MongoDB document as the mapper stores it, and a ! line for every query, update, index, sort, projection or @Query string that names a field the document does not have (verification pending)
commits.body:
A Criteria.where("expiresAt"), an Update.set("status", ...), an Index().on("holdId", ASC), a Sort.by("createdAt") or a repository @Query("{ 'customerId': ?0 }") names a field as a string, and nothing checks the string: the driver sends it to the database, which matches, writes, indexes or sorts by whatever field that is. A renamed record component leaves every query of it matching nothing and every test that goes through the same strings passing. The new module lib/src/store.rs renders each @Document class of the module as a 'stored' block (the @Id or the property named id as _id, a @Field rename as 'due: Instant (dueAt)', @Transient and transient fields left out, the superclass's fields first, each embedded local type as its own 'record, embedded' block) and, under the document, a ! line for every field-name string in the module's bytecode and annotations that names a field it does not have: Criteria.where/and, the Update write and remove operators, Index.on, Sort.by (varargs read back from the array the compiler builds), Sort.Order, the projection's include/exclude, a repository method's @Query value/sort/fields (parsed as the loose JSON Spring accepts, with the $ operators transparent) and a document's @CompoundIndex definition. A string may use the Java or the stored name of a property, _id or the id property's name, a dotted path through embedded types, collections and maps, with $ segments and array indices skipped; a path into a leaf type (a String, an Instant, an enum) is a problem too. The document a string is about is the one the method names (a class literal passed to the template, or a new of the document); a helper that names none takes its callers' documents, and a string with none in reach is checked against every document of the module. The nearest property is suggested when it is within a few edits. commits.summary: Add reach lines to boundary contracts: under each entry point what it reads, writes, sends, calls and publishes, from a call graph over the application's own classes, with a ! line for a GET with side effects and a read-only transaction that writes (verification pending)
commits.body:
A boundary contract listed where Spring enters a module and what advice applies, but not what an entry point does. The new module lib/src/reach.rs follows the calls in the bytecode from each entry point and advised method through the application's own classes (the module and its sibling modules; a call into Spring, the JDK or a driver is a leaf) and classifies the leaves: the Spring Data templates and repositories, the JPA EntityManager and the JDBC helpers give reads and writes (of the class literal passed, else the static type of the entity argument, else the documents the method mentions; a table from the SQL constant), the Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, Spring Cloud Stream and AWS templates give sends, RestTemplate, RestClient, WebClient and @HttpExchange or Feign interfaces give HTTP calls, ApplicationEventPublisher gives events. Virtual calls go to every local subtype that overrides the method, lambdas to their bodies through the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap arguments. The lines go under the entry point as details (reads A, B / writes C / sends t / calls GET /x / publishes E). Two checks read them: a GET or HEAD route that writes, sends, publishes or makes a non-GET call is a ! line (a safe method with side effects), and a @Transactional(readOnly = true) method that writes is a ! line. The stack walk in boundaries::pushing now goes through dup, so a new X(...) argument is typed.

Verified by the library's Spring fixtures (new TaskFlow, TasksController, Work, Notifier, KafkaNotifier, UserClient and TaskCreated, with stubs for KafkaTemplate, JdbcTemplate, RestClient, ApplicationEventPublisher and the HttpExchange annotations): one path of each kind, the two problems, and a handler that reaches nothing; 90 unit and 29 integration tests pass. commits.summary: Place each reach effect with respect to transactions: a send or an HTTP call from inside a transaction (a dual write), an event published outside one that a @TransactionalEventListener waits for, and an after-commit listener that writes are ! lines (verification pending)
commits.body: The reach lines of a boundary contract now carry a transaction scope along the walk from each entry point (lib/src/reach.rs): an effect is reached with no transaction on the path, inside a transaction the method opens (its own @Transactional, or a lambda it hands to TransactionTemplate.execute or to a helper that reaches it, such as Box Office's Transactions.run), or inside a @Transactional method of another class, which accounts for its own effects, so a ! line sits under the service method and not under every route that calls it. Four checks in lib/src/boundaries.rs read the placement: a transaction that sends to a topic, exchange or queue (the dual write an outbox exists to avoid; left alone when spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix makes the Kafka producer transactional), a transaction that makes an HTTP call, an event published with no transaction while a @TransactionalEventListener of the module or a sibling waits for it (Spring drops the event), and a @TransactionalEventListener in a phase after the commit whose reach writes without REQUIRES_NEW or @Async (nothing commits again, so a JPA or JDBC write is never committed). Verified by the Spring fixtures (new TaskAudit listeners, Work.atomically through a TransactionTemplate stub, TaskFlow.rename and close, two new routes; 90 unit and 29 integration tests pass) and by the three Box Office contracts, which regenerate unchanged. Example 117 replaces the outbox in OrderService.place with a direct KafkaTemplate send from inside Transactions.run; confirmed by hand with the Gradle verifyBoundaries task: POST /orders gains sends payments.commands and the dual-write ! line. commits.summary: Add request binding checks to boundary contracts: a @PathVariable whose name is a variable of no template of its route, a binder whose parameter name the compiler did not record, a required = false binder on a primitive, two @RequestBody parameters, and two handlers on one route are ! lines (verification pending)
commits.body:
A handler's parameters bind to the request at request time, by a name Spring takes from the annotation or from the bytecode, so a mismatch is neither a compile error nor a startup failure but a 500 on every request of the route, which the unit tests of the service do not make. The new module lib/src/binding.rs reads each handler's @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue and @MatrixVariable against the route templates and the class file: a @PathVariable whose name (the annotation's value or name, else the parameter's as the MethodParameters attribute records it) is a variable of no template of the route is MissingPathVariableException; a binder with no name of its own on a parameter whose name is not in that attribute (no javac -parameters; Spring 6.1 no longer reads the LocalVariableTable) fails every request; a required = false binder with no defaultValue on a primitive cannot be given null; a second @RequestBody always reads an empty body. Two handlers on one route are found across the module: the same route on two methods, which Spring refuses at startup, and the same pattern under different variable names, which both match every such request with the same specificity, so Spring raises an ambiguity for it. Method::reflective_parameter_names exposes the MethodParameters names on their own, and parameter_names uses it.

Verified by the integration fixtures: TasksController gains DELETE /tasks/{taskId} with @PathVariable String id and GET /tasks/page with @RequestParam(required = false) int page, a new TaskSearchController claims GET /tasks/open (identical to TasksController.open) and GET /tasks/{key}/owner (the pattern of TasksController.owner), and a new fixture set tests/fixtures/spring-legacy is compiled without -parameters so that its @PathVariable id has no name Spring can see while its @RequestParam("q") and Map parameter need none; the contract has the expected ! line under each and the counts are (30 beans, 27 entry points, 65 problems). 92 unit tests and 29 integration tests pass. The four Box Office boundary contracts regenerate unchanged: every @PathVariable names a variable of its route, the modules compile with -parameters, no two handlers share a pattern. Example 118 renames the variable of HoldController's GET /holds/{id} template to {holdId} and leaves the parameter as it was; with the patch applied, ./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun reports the renamed route with the ! line (@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}: MissingPathVariableException, a 500 on every request) and 1 problem. The example's pipeline run is job 20261103-072635-example-118-the-hold-route-s-path-variab. commits.summary: Add throws lines to boundary contracts: under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes (the @ExceptionHandler that takes it and its status, a @ResponseStatus, a ResponseStatusException's status, or a 500), with ! lines for an exception of the module's own that nothing maps and for two handlers of one type in one advice (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract's boundary contract now lists under each entry point the exceptions it can throw, found over the same call graph as the reach lines: the throw statements (a new, a typed local, what a method returned or a cast produced), the suppliers of Optional.orElseThrow and Spring's Assert calls in everything the entry point reaches, less what a catch on the path takes without rethrowing (a handler that rethrows its variable, such as a finally or the retry loop in Box Office's Transactions.run, passes everything through; one that wraps throws the wrapper); an @Async callee of another class throws on its own thread, and the compiler's own MatchException and assert are left out. For a route each exception is followed by what Spring makes of it, in Spring's order: the @ExceptionHandler in the controller or in a @ControllerAdvice (by @Order, matched by its packages, types and annotations, the closest type winning) with the status it answers (its @ResponseStatus, the first HttpStatus constant its body loads, or the literal it passes to ResponseEntity.status), the @ResponseStatus on the exception's class, the status a ResponseStatusException was built with, or (500). An exception type of the module's own that nothing maps is a ! line; a JDK or framework exception is listed as a 500 without one, since a guard that fired is a 500 by design. Two @ExceptionHandler methods for one type in one advice are a ! line too (Spring refuses the ambiguity at startup). A listener, a schedule or a bean method gets its throws line without outcomes. New module lib/src/failures.rs; Graph::throws in lib/src/reach.rs with the per-method throw and catch analysis.

commits.summary: Regression proofs share the callees both versions call unchanged, and skip a target whose bytecode is identical (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract equivalence now compares the two versions' bytecode before any solver runs (lib/src/shared.rs). A target identical in both versions, together with everything it reaches (instructions compared with their constant pool references resolved, exception tables, the static initializers and constant values of the classes whose statics it reads), is verified with nothing to prove and no JBMC run. A callee both versions call unchanged, that is a pure function of its primitive arguments (no fields, no arrays, nothing of the JDK beyond Math/StrictMath/Integer/Long/Short/Byte, string building and the exceptions it constructs), is taken as one function in both versions, the uninterpreted-function abstraction of regression verification: a generated stub class (SharedCallees, the class writer now writes static fields) keeps a memo table per callee, giving arguments seen before the outcome they got and new arguments an arbitrary result or one of the exceptions the callee can throw (its new'ed Throwables, plus ArithmeticException where it divides), and the invokestatic call sites of both versions are redirected to it by appending constant pool entries and rewriting the operands in place. The solver then relates how the versions use the callee and never its arithmetic. The abstraction is sound for a proof; a counterexample found with it is replayed through the real bytecode and, when it does not reproduce, the proof is run again with the callees as written, with a note. --no-shared-callees turns both off. The proof line names the callees taken as one function; Outcome gains a shared field.

Why: a 64-bit division in a helper both versions call was what turned a regression proof of a caller into a time-out, since each version carried its own copy for the solver to relate. Measured: a refactor of a caller around a division helper went from not finishing in 60 s to a proof in 0.2 s, and HoldPolicy-style pricing with Math.multiplyExact shared from 3.4 s to 0.4 s.

Example 120 on Crosscut: a new kernel, ratelimit.RetryAfter#nanosUntilToken (the Retry-After of a refused request, from TokenBucket's refill helpers), with a test, a property proved in 1.7 s, and the API contract regenerated; the example's patch rewrites the wait as the period less the time since the credit, around the unchanged helpers. By hand: proved in 1.3 s with the helpers shared; without sharing the [-100000:100000] search stage had not finished after 60 s. New technique tag shared-callees. Docs: lib README (proof steps and limits), approaches.md B9, the Crosscut README, the plugin reference; build.py reads the 'nothing to prove' proof line.

commits.summary: Regression proofs across a signature change: the previous version named and called with expressions over the new parameters (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract equivalence proved a method only against a previous version of the same name and parameters; a method renamed, moved, or whose parameters were reordered, added, removed or retyped could not be proved at all. Now --before-target names the previous method (pkg.Class#method) and --before-arguments gives its arguments as expressions over the new parameters (tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB; start, (int) (end - start), failed; an array by name), and the statement proved is new(x) agrees with old(f(x)). The harness (lib/src/harness/mod.rs, BeforeMethod) type-checks each expression against the parameter it is passed as with the expression language's call syntax, narrows for byte/short/char and widens for long, computes the arguments into locals inside a handler that skips an input the mapping throws on, and calls the relocated previous method; the Java rendering shows the mapping. equivalence.rs resolves the previous method in the old classes and refuses clearly when the class or method is missing, is not static, returns another type, or when the parameters differ with no mapping given; the proof line reads 'behaves as the previous winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB) on every input', a counterexample is shown as both versions received it ('winner(tsA=0, tsB=0, nodeA=0, nodeB=0), previously winner(tsA=0, nodeA=0, tsB=0, nodeB=0)'), the replay maps the arguments through the interpreter, and the JSON outcome carries the previous call. shared::plan takes both targets and uses the identical-bytecode shortcut only for the plain statement, since f(a, b) against f(b, a) on identical bytecode proves nothing. The tool's own checker handles the mapped harness unchanged.

Example 121 (B9, Quorum): LastWriterWins#winner regrouped as (tsA, tsB, nodeA, nodeB) and written as a Long.compare/Integer.compare chain, with the test and the law in properties.contract updated in the patch; example.json carries change.previousArguments, which build.py passes to the tool (change.previousSymbol maps to --before-target; schema and page rendering extended); new technique tag signature-change. Job 20261104-061118-example-121-a-tie-break-s-parameters-reg is queued. Verified: 97 unit tests (one new, the harness with a mapping) and 37 integration tests (four new on a Writers fixture: a reordering proved, a moved and renamed method proved, a tie rewrite found with the mapped counterexample, a refusal without a mapping), clippy clean on the changed files, the patched Quorum tree compiles and its 58 tests pass, the mapped proof and counterexample reproduced under --engine native, release binary installed. Documented in lib/README.md, the plugin reference, examples/approaches.md, examples/README.md and Quorum's README.

commits.summary: Regression proofs under a stated relation between the results: a result that changed its type or meaning is related to the previous one with --results-agree-when (verification pending)
commits.body:
A regression proof compared what the two versions return, so a method whose return type changed, or whose result changed its meaning (a boolean that became the time left, nanoseconds that became milliseconds), could not be proved against its previous version. jvmcontract equivalence now takes --results-agree-when EXPR, a boolean expression over the new parameters, previous (the previous version's result) and result (the new one's), which takes the place of equality whenever both versions return; the versions must still throw alike, array parameters are still compared, and a relation that throws on a pair of results does not hold. The expression is type-checked against both return types, compiled into the generated harness (lib/src/harness/mod.rs, BeforeMethod::parse_relation, Harness.relation) and rendered in the Java statement written for readers. Differing return types are refused without a relation, with a message that names the flag. The identical-bytecode shortcut and the shared-callee plan are off under a relation, since identical code proves nothing about it. A counterexample is replayed in the interpreter and the relation evaluated on the replayed results (lib/src/equivalence.rs, Replays), so that a JBMC counterexample a missing model produced is still recognised as not reproducing; the report adds the line 'the results are not related by ...' under the two outcomes, and the JSON outcome carries the relation.

Examples 122 and 123 on Crosscut's cache expiry: Expiry#isExpired, a boolean, turned into the time an entry has left, related by previousSymbol and resultsAgreeWhen 'previous == (result <= 0)' with the module's own precondition as the scope (outside it the new subtraction overflows). 123 (remainingNanos) is expected verified; 122 (remainingMillis) is expected to show an entry with a fraction of a millisecond to go reported expired, since the integer division rounds it to no millisecond. The example runner passes change.resultsAgreeWhen to the tool (examples/tools/build.py, examples/schema/example.schema.json), and the pages, lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the Crosscut README and the verify-bytecode skill reference describe the flag.
